bible_refs.note: Lemma quoted three times: Νόμος δὲ παρεισῆλθεν ἵνα πλεονάσῃ τὸ παράπτωμα; and Οὗ δὲ ἐπλεόνασεν ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις.
LXX Psalm 13:3 (also quoted in Romans 3:12); Hebrew/English numbering 14:3. Cyril reads ἦν for LXX ἔστιν.
διεφθάρκασι ... τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτῶν echoes LXX κατέφθειρεν πᾶσα σὰρξ τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; the flood follows in the next clause.
New lemma: Ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι ὅσοι ἐβαπτίσθημεν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν.
εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος.
ἐν Πατρὶ ὁ Υἱός, ἐν Υἱῷ ὁ Πατήρ, echoing ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί (also John 14:11).

choices.english: the law was brought in between
choices.why: τὸ δέ Παρεισῆλθεν, ἀντὶ τοῦ παρεισβέβληκε: Cyril glosses the verb; rendered as 'the law was brought in between', keeping his point that it stands between Adam's condemnation and Christ's righteousness.
πρόξενος: 'one who brings about, procures'; rendered 'promoter of sin'.

choices.term: ἰδικῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ κατὰ χώρας τε καὶ πόλεις

choices.why: ἰδικῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ κατὰ χώρας τε καὶ πόλεις: the verb ἐκολάζοντο is carried over from the previous clause ('they were also punished in particular ways').

pass_a_gloss: εἶτα ποία ... ἡ χρεία: then what need (χρεία), as of necessity (ἐξ ἀνάγκης), of the laws through Moses? πρὸς τὰ τοιαῦτα: against such things the divine (θεσπέσιος) Paul all but (μονονουχί) stands up (ἀνίσταται) saying: law came in beside (παρεισῆλθεν) that the trespass (παράπτωμα) might abound (πλεονάσῃ). 'came in beside' = instead of 'was thrown in between' (παρεισβέβληκε μεταξύ) the condemnation (κατάκρισις) in Adam and the righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) in Christ. what need of the law's running-in (παρεισδρομή) one will hear him clearly saying: that the trespass might abound. what do you say, O Paul? was the law also procurer (πρόξενος) of sin, and has the trespass multiplied (πεπλήθυνται) through it? may it not be (μὴ γένοιτο). must widen (κατευρῦναι) the manner of the mystagogy (μυσταγωγία). David said: all turned aside (ἐξέκλιναν), together became useless (ἠχρειώθησαν), there was not one doing kindness/good (χρηστότητα), not even one. for all on earth had corrupted (διεφθάρκασι) their way after the transgression (παράβασις) in Adam; therefore they were punished (ἐκολάζοντο), all enduring a common penalty (δίκη), the flood (κατακλυσμός), and particularly (ἰδικῶς) by times and by lands and cities. for even if there was no law, yet from implanted motions (ἐμφύτων κινημάτων) human nature was being tutored (ἐπαιδαγωγεῖτο) by God toward knowledge (εἴδησις) of good things. those on earth having fared wretchedly God pitied (κατηλέει), and kindly (φιλαγάθως) considered freeing them in Christ from the tyrannizing sin; but thought it needful, and very rightly, that those on earth be first shown (προαναφαίνεσθαι) much sick (νοσοῦντας), so that the justification (δικαίωσις) in Christ, having a most needful entry into the world, might be seen thereafter. for we say not the already just is justified (δικαιοῦσθαι), but whoever is liable (ἔνοχος) to sins. how then must those on earth be shown beforehand as needing the grace in Christ? law came in that the trespass might abound: that is, that among those under law the trespass might appear great, none being able to be justified because of nature's weakness (ἀσθενές), all as it were falling under the charges (αἰτίαι) from transgression. so the law was set as a kind of proof/exposure (ἔλεγχος) of the weakness of all, so that human things appear needing only the healing (θεραπεία) through Christ. therefore he says: where sin abounded grace super-abounded (ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν). for it had to be so great as to appear better than the condemning law. [lemma] or do you not know that as many as were baptized into Christ Jesus? we have been baptized admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; if he says we were baptized into Christ Jesus, he will not speak outside the fitting (εἰκότος). for by names and hypostases (ὑποστάσεσι) and differences of persons (προσώπων διαφοραῖς) the Father will stand apart (διεστήξει) somehow into particular otherness (ἰδικὴν ἑτερότητα) toward the Son and the Spirit toward both; for the Father is Father and not Son; Son again by nature (κατὰ φύσιν) the one from him and not Father; Spirit particularly the Holy Spirit. since the Son is in the Father, the Father in the Son, the Holy Spirit being in both on account of the sameness (ταὐτόν) of substance (οὐσία), even if one names one, by force of the concepts (δυνάμει θεωρημάτων) the declaration (δήλωσις) of the whole [continues: ἐποιήσατο, u03-open]
pass_b_english: …What need, then, was there, as a matter of necessity, for the laws given through Moses? Against such thoughts the inspired Paul all but rises up again, saying, “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20). The words “came in” mean that the law was brought in between the condemnation in Adam and the righteousness in Christ. And if one asks again what need there was for the law’s coming in, he will hear Paul say plainly, “So that the trespass might increase.” What are you saying, Paul? Was the law, then, also a promoter of sin, and has the trespass multiplied through it? By no means.

We must, then, open out more fully the way this sacred teaching works. David said, accordingly, “All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there was none who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 14:3). For after the transgression in Adam all who were on the earth had corrupted their way (Genesis 6:12). That is why they were punished: all of them together underwent a common penalty, the flood, and they were also punished in particular ways, at certain times and in certain lands and cities. For even though there was no law, human nature was still being trained by God, through its inborn impulses, toward the knowledge of what is good.

So God took pity on those on earth, who were faring wretchedly, and in his love of goodness he planned to set them free in Christ from the sin that tyrannized them. But he judged, and very rightly, that those on earth must first be shown to be gravely sick, so that the justification in Christ might then be seen to make its entry into the world as something most needed. For we say that it is not the one already righteous who is justified, but whoever is liable for sins. How, then, were those on earth to be shown beforehand as needing the grace that is in Christ? “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20); that is, so that among those under the law the trespass might appear great, since plainly no one could be justified because of the weakness of nature, and all, as it were, fell under the charges that arise from transgression. The law, then, was laid down as a kind of proof of the weakness of all, so that human affairs might be seen to need the healing that comes through Christ alone. That is why he says, “But where sin increased, grace overflowed all the more” (Romans 5:20). For grace had to be so great that it would be seen to surpass the law that condemns.

“Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus…?” (Romans 6:3). As all agree, we have been baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Yet if he should say that we have been baptized into Christ Jesus, he will not be speaking beyond what is reasonable. It is quite true that by names, by hypostases, and by the differences of the persons, the Father stands apart from the Son in a certain particular otherness, and the Spirit from both. For the Father is the Father and not the Son; again, the one who is from him by nature is the Son and not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is, in his own proper way, the Spirit. But since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son (John 14:10), and the Holy Spirit is in both because the substance is the same, then even if someone names only one, by the force of the ideas involved, the declaration of the whole…

εἶτα ποία γέγονε τῶν διὰ Μωυσέως νόμων ὡς ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἡ χρεία; πρὸς δὴ τὰ τοιαῦτα
πάλιν ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος μονονουχὶ καὶ ἀνίσταται λέγων Νόμος δὲ παρεισῆλθεν ἵνα
πλεονάσῃ τὸ παράπτωμα· τὸ δέ Παρεισῆλθεν, ἀντὶ τοῦ παρεισβέβληκε μεταξὺ τῆς τε ἐν
Ἀδὰμ κατακρίσεως καὶ τὴς ἐν Χριστῷ δικαιοσύνης. καὶ τίς ἂν νοοῖτο πάλιν τῆς τοῦ
νόμου παρεισδρομῆς ἡ χρεία, σαφῶς ἀκούσει λέγοντος Ἵνα πλεονάσῃ τὸ παράπτωμα. τί
φῂς, ὦ Παῦλε; ἆρα καὶ ἁμαρτίας ὁ νόμος ἦν πρόξενος, καὶ πεπλήθυνται δι' αὐτοῦ τὸ
παράπτωμα; μὴ γένοιτο. χρὴ τοίνυν κατευρῦναι τῆς μυσταγωγίας τὸν τρόπον. ἔφη
τοιγαροῦν ὁ ∆αυεὶδ ὅτι "πάντες ἐξέκλιναν, ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν, οὐκ ἦν ὁ ποιῶν
χρη"στότητα, οὐκ ἦν ἕως ἑνός·" διεφθάρκασι μὲν γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς τὴν ὁδὸν
αὐτῶν μετὰ τὴν ἐν Ἀδὰμ παράβασιν· ταύτῃτοι καὶ ἐκολάζοντο, κοινὴν μὲν ἅπαντες
ὑπομείναντες δίκην τὸν κατακλυσμὸν, ἰδικῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ κατὰ χώρας τε
καὶ πόλεις· εἰ γὰρ καὶ νόμος οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλ' οὖν 188 καὶ ἐξ ἐμφύτων κινημάτων
ἐπαιδαγωγεῖτο παρὰ Θεοῦ πρὸς εἴδησιν τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἡ ἀνθρώπου φύσις. πεπραχότας δὴ
οὖν ἀθλίως τοὺς ἐπὶ γῆς κατηλέει Θεὸς, καὶ τῆς τυραννούσης αὐτοὺς ἁμαρτίας
ἀπαλλάττειν ἐν Χριστῷ φιλαγάθως ἐσκέπτετο· ἀλλὰ δεῖν ᾠήθη καὶ μάλα ὀρθῶς πολὺ
νοσοῦντας προαναφαίνεσθαι τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἵνα χρειωδεστάτην ἔχουσα τὴν εἰς τὸν
κόσμον εἰσβολὴν, ἡ ἐν Χριστῷ δικαίωσις ὁρῷτο λοιπόν· δικαιοῦσθαι γάρ φαμεν οὐ τὸν
ἤδη δίκαιον, ἀλλ' εἴ τις ἐστὶν ἁμαρτίαις ἔνοχος· πῶς οὖν ἔδει προαναδείκνυσθαι τοὺς
ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ χάριτος δεδεημένους; παρεισῆλθε νόμος ἵνα πλεονάσῃ τὸ
παράπτωμα· τουτέστιν, ἵνα ἐν τοῖς ὑπὸ νόμον πολὺ φαίνοιτο τὸ παράπτωμα, μηδενὸς
δηλονότι δικαιοῦσθαι δυναμένου διὰ τὸ τῆς φύσεως ἀσθενὲς, ὑποπιπτόντων δὲ ὥσπερ
ἁπάντων ταῖς ἐκ παραβάσεως αἰτίαις. τέθειται τοίνυν ὁ νόμος ἔλεγχος οἷά τις τῆς
ἁπάντων ἀσθενείας, ἵνα φαίνοιτο τὰ ἀνθρώπινα μόνης τῆς διὰ Χριστοῦ θεραπείας
δεδεημένα· ταύτῃτοί φησιν Οὗ δὲ ἐπλεόνασεν ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις· ἔδει
γὰρ εἶναι τοσαύτην ὡς ἀμείνω φαίνεσθαι τοῦ κατακρίνοντος νόμου. Ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι
ὅσοι ἐβαπτίσθημεν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν; Βεβαπτίσμεθα μὲν ὁμολογουμένως εἰς τὸ ὄνομα
τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος· εἰ δὲ δὴ λέγοι ὡς εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν
βεβαπτίσμεθα, οὐκ ἔξω τοῦ εἰκότος ἐρεῖ· μάλιστα μὲν γὰρ ὀνόμασί τε καὶ ὑποστάσεσι καὶ
προσώπων διαφοραῖς εἰς ἰδικὴν ἑτερότητα διεστήξει πως Πατὴρ πρὸς Υἱὸν καὶ πρὸς
ἄμφω τὸ Πνεῦμα· Πατὴρ γάρ ἐστιν ὁ Πατὴρ καὶ οὐχ Υἱός· Υἱὸς δ' αὖ πάλιν κατὰ φύσιν ὁ
ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ οὐ Πατὴρ, Πνεῦμα δὲ ἰδικῶς τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον· ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἐν Πατρὶ μέν
ἐστιν ὁ Υἱὸς, ἐν Υἱῷ δὲ Πατὴρ, ὄντος ἐν ἀμφοῖν τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος διὰ τὸ τῆς οὐσίας

reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged new translation checked clause by clause against the source: complete, senses, negation, the μὴ γένοιτο, the Trinitarian terms (hypostases, persons, substance) and all citations (Romans 5:20 x3; Psalm 14:3 = LXX 13:3; Genesis 6:12; Romans 6:3; Matthew 28:19; John 14:10) are correct. One fix in the staging file: 'What need could there have been' changed to 'What need, then, was there' (γέγονε is a plain past, not a potential). The seam with the retranslated u02-rem-mid (objector's question) reads correctly.

Opens mid-argument: εἶτα ποία ... ἡ χρεία finishes the objector's question begun at the end of u02-rem-mid (if justification in Christ was to appear with nothing in between, why the Mosaic law?). The leading ellipsis marks the join.
Ends mid-sentence: the main verb ἐποιήσατο stands at the start of u03-open; the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing supplied.
PG column numbers 188 and 189 and the page number 6 in the copy-text are dropped from the reading text.

τὸ δέ Παρεισῆλθεν, ἀντὶ τοῦ παρεισβέβληκε: Cyril glosses the verb; rendered as 'the law was brought in between', keeping his point that it stands between Adam's condemnation and Christ's righteousness.
πρόξενος: 'one who brings about, procures'; rendered 'promoter of sin'.
ἰδικῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ κατὰ χώρας τε καὶ πόλεις: the verb ἐκολάζοντο is carried over from the previous clause ('they were also punished in particular ways').
The Trinitarian sentence keeps Cyril's terms: ὑποστάσεσι = hypostases, προσώπων = persons, οὐσίας = substance. ἰδικὴν ἑτερότητα = 'particular otherness'.
Subject of λέγοι ('if he should say') is Paul, left as 'he' as in the Greek.
